newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers' strike aggravates Juppe's woes.
newsitem.headline: French truckers' strike aggravates Juppe's woes.

text.p: France's 12-day-old truckers' strike has put the spotlight on the dwindling authority of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's government, already hit by a slump in popularity and feuding over European monetary union.

"Who's in charge?" the popular daily Le Parisien asked in a front-page headline on Friday, pointing to a widespread sense of drift in France and saying that the centre-right government was clearly unable to control labour unrest.

Employers and unions have both sought to exploit Juppe's weakness to press the government into signing cheques to resolve the strike, which is slowly throttling the French economy with about 230 roadblocks on major roads.

Most of the concessions in this private sector dispute have so far been made by the state, which has agreed to lower payroll charges for employers and help to finance early retirement for truckers at 55 instead of 60. It is now poised to settle the issue of drivers' working hours by decree.

Juppe said on Thursday a solution was urgent, cautioning that "the consequences (of a prolonged strike) on our economy, on many companies, on many workers risk being very damaging". His past appeals have gone unheeded.

In recent months, the government has seemed resigned to undertaking day-to-day management rather than putting forward grand designs, fearful of stirring up unions who staged a crippling 24-day strike late last year against welfare reform plans.
Political commentator Alain Duhamel said President Jacques Chirac, who has not addressed the nation since July, should speak out on television before Christmas to try to restore a sense of direction.
"One can wonder if such a long absence, such a breakdown of communication, may not be contributing to the feeling of drift which adds to French anxieties today," he wrote in the daily Liberation.
Stephane Rozes, head of political studies at the CSA polling institute, agreed. "We are facing a communication vacuum from the top," he said.
"The public doesn't understand what principles are guiding France. Two-thirds of the French people want faster growth even if it worsens public sector deficits," he told Reuters.
Juppe, shown by opinion polls to be the least popular premier in modern history, was a scapegoat for all France's woes while Chirac stayed out of sight or travelled abroad, Rozes said.

The government, long under fire from disgruntled parliamentary backbenchers who fear a rout in the next elections in 1998, also faces an open challenge to its European Union policy from former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing.

Backbenchers from Juppe's Gaullist party applauded Giscard d'Estaing, a member of the centre-right UDF, in parliament this week when he called for a depreciation of the franc to help boost jobs and growth to prepare for a single European currency.
Juppe ruled out devaluation and said France would push ahead with budget deficit-cutting required to qualify for monetary union in 1999.

The gloom, with mounting calls for a cabinet reshuffle, is set to mar celebrations at the weekend of the anniversary of the Rally for the Republic Party (RPR), founded by Chirac in 1976 and now led by Juppe.
Despite opinion polls showing the popularity of Juppe and Chirac at or near rock bottom, the anniversary posters proclaim the RPR is celebrating: "Twenty years in love with France."
